The vertical modes are engaged and disengaged through the related pushbuttons on the Flight Control Panel (FCP). When a vertical Mode is selected, incompatible Modes will be automatically deselected. The Autoflight System controls the following vertical modes:
*   **Pitch (PTCH) Mode:** Hold preselected pitch angle.
*   **Altitude Select (ALTS) Mode:** Capture preselected barometric altitude.
*   **Altitude Hold Mode (ALT):** Hold current barometric altitude.
*   **Vertical Speed Mode (VS):** Hold preselected vertical speed.
*   **Flight Level Change (FLC) Mode:** Hold airspeed or Mach number during climb or descent.
*   **Vertical Navigation (VNAV) Mode:** FMS automatically selects ALTS, ALT, VS, FLC, Path, or Glidepath.
*   **Approach (APPR) Mode - Glideslope (GS) Mode:** Descend in accordance with the glideslope signal or the FMS command.
*   **Takeoff (TO) Mode:** Vertical guidance based on takeoff target speed.
*   **Go-around (GA) Mode:** Vertical guidance based on go-around target speed.
*   **Overspeed (OSPD) Mode:** Hold fixed indicated airspeed or Mach number.
*   **Underspeed (USPD) Mode:** Hold fixed indicated airspeed or Mach number.
*   **Windshear Escape Mode (WS):** Hold specified pitch angle and airspeed.

VNAV CLIMB allows the aircraft to climb to each constraint altitude and hold that altitude until the constraint is cleared. It honors only climb constraints during the climb phase. Depending on the constraint type (AT, AT OR BELOW, BETWEEN, or AT OR ABOVE), VNAV will either hold the specified altitude until the waypoint is reached, hold the higher altitude for BETWEEN constraints, or impose no holding requirement for AT OR ABOVE constraints.

In the climb phase, VNAV allows the aircraft to climb to each constraint altitude and hold that altitude until the constraint is cleared. VNAV honors only climb constraints. If an altitude constraint requires crossing a waypoint at the specified altitude or at or below it, the specified altitude is held until the waypoint is reached. If the constraint is between two altitudes, the higher altitude is held. If the constraint is at or above a specified altitude, there is no requirement to hold an altitude.

The climb phase is entered whenever the flight plan target altitude and the preselect altitude are set above the altitude of the aircraft, and the autopilot is in an altitude change mode (FLC, VS, or PTCH).

During the climb phase, VNAV honors only climb constraints. VNAV allows the aircraft to climb to each constraint altitude and hold that altitude until the constraint is cleared. If the altitude constraint requires the aircraft to cross the waypoint at the specified altitude, or at or below the specified altitude, the specified altitude is held until the waypoint is reached. If the altitude constraint requires the aircraft to cross the waypoint between two altitudes, the higher altitude is held. If the altitude constraint requires the aircraft to cross the waypoint at or above the specified altitude, then there is no requirement to hold an altitude.
VNAV provides speed and altitude targets consistent with the climb constraints and speed limits.

Responses: Stall alert, stall protection and auto-ignition functions.
Only when both SPC's generate stall pusher commands at the same time, will the stick pusher activate.

The STALL ADVANCE Switch, when pushed and its ON light illuminates, activates the ADVANCE ON Mode of the Stall Protection System (SPS). When released, it is a condition for activating Ice Advance Modes 1, 2, and 3. Manually pushing the STALL ADVANCE Switch while in Ice Advance Mode 2 causes the system to enter ADVANCE ON Mode, while releasing it can revert the system to normal mode or ADVANCE ON Mode based on current status.

In ADVANCE ON Mode, the Stall Protection System (SPS) drives the stall alert (stick vibration, STALL aural alert and the warning flag on the PFD). The stick pusher reduces when the AOA returns to normal condition. This enhances the stall protection margin. The stall alert, stall protection and auto-ignition AOA threshold will be enhanced. EICAS triggers the cyan SPS ADVANCE ON Mode CAS message.
SPS ADVANCE ON Mod

The stick pusher is activated when the current AOA of the aircraft reaches a threshold value for stall protection, and only when both Stall Protection Computers (SPCs) generate stall pusher commands simultaneously. Its activation is controlled by the pitch servo, driven by the elevator, via commands sent from the SPCs to the autoflight system.

The Stall Protection System (SPS) has multiple modes including Flap/Slat System Fail Advance Mode, ADVANCE ON Mode, Ice Advance Mode 3, Ice Advance Mode 2, Ice Advance Mode 1 and normal Mode. ADVANCE ON Mode activates if the STALL ADVANCE Switch is pushed and the ON light illuminates. Ice Advance Mode 1 activates when ice is detected on either side and the wing anti-ice system is available and the STALL ADVANCE Switch is released. Ice Advance Mode 2 activates when ice is detected on either side, the wing anti-ice system fails, and the STALL ADVANCE Switch is released. Ice Advance Mode 3 activates when ice is detected on either side, the wing anti-ice system is available, the WING A/I Switch is pushed, and the STALL ADVANCE Switch is released. Flap/Slat Fail Advance Mode activates if the flap system fails on the FSECU bus and the flap configuration is not in 0, or if the flap system fails on the FSECU bus or slat angle is unavailable on both sides and flap configuration is not in 0, or if the slat angle difference between the two sides is 3° for 5 seconds and flap configuration is not in 0.

Underspeed (USPD) Mode is automatically activated if a significant low speed occurs. It generates pitch commands to increase airspeed above Vman or Mman. When airspeed/Mach exceeds Vman/Mman, USPD Mode deactivates, and the airspeed reference is set to Vman + 5 kt/Mman + 0.01. The FG vertical Mode switches to FLC Mode while the current altitude reference is maintained. The SPEED Knob is inhibited, and other vertical modes are inhibited unless in ALTS, ALT, TO, or GA Mode. The purpose of Pitch (PTCH) Mode is to hold the actual aircraft pitch angle at the time of mode selection. PTCH Mode is activated automatically when the Autoflight System is energized and the FD is engaged for the first time, or if no other vertical modes are selected. Engaging the AP with both FDs disengaged will also activate PTCH Mode. PTCH Mode can be activated and the pitch angle reference changed by turning the PITCH/VS Wheel when in ALTS, ALT, FLC, GA, PATH Angle, GP, or OSPD (when not in overspeed status) Modes. The PTCH Mode is disengaged when another vertical mode is selected, as incompatible modes are automatically deselected.

The Autoflight System controls the following vertical modes: Vertical Modes Meaning Pitch (PTCH) Mode Hold preselected pitch angle. Altitude Select (ALTS) Mode Capture preselected barometric altitude. Altitude Hold Mode (ALT) Hold current barometric altitude. Vertical Speed Mode (VS) Hold preselected vertical speed. Flight Level Change (FLC) Mode Hold airspeed or Mach number during climb or descent. Vertical Navigation (VNAV) Mode FMS select the Mode of ALTS, ALT, VS, FLC, Path or Glidepath automatically. Approach (APPR) Mode - Glideslope (GS) Mode Descend in accordance with the glideslope signal or the FMS command. Takeoff (TO) Mode - Vertical Guidance based on takeoff target speed. Go-around (GA) Mode - Vertical Guidance based on go-around target speed. Overspeed (OSPD) Mode Hold fixed indicated airspeed or Mach number. Vertical Modes Meaning Underspeed (USPD) Mode Hold fixed indicated airspeed or Mach number. Windshear Escape Mode (WS) Hold specified pitch angle and airspeed.
The GS Mode generates commands to capture or track the selected glideslope. In the APPR Mode, the AT controls airspeed.
Takeoff (TO) Mode - Vertical provides guidance based on takeoff target speed, while Go-around (GA) Mode - Vertical provides guidance based on go-around target speed.

The Overspeed (OSPD) Mode is activated when the aircraft Mach number exceeds Mmo + 0.01 or airspeed exceeds Vmo + 5 kt. It generates pitch commands to reduce airspeed below Vmo/Mmo, with a speed reference of Mmo - 0.02 or Vmo - 10 kt. The Underspeed (USPD) Mode activates during significant low speed events and generates pitch commands to increase airspeed above Vman or Mman, with a speed reference of Vman + 5 kt/Mman +0.01. In both modes, the Automatic Thrust (AT) is armed to control engine thrust/speed and the SPEED Knob is inhibited.

Responses: VNAV CLIMB
The VNAV CLIMB page shows the default setting for Target Speed, Transition Altitude and Speed/Altitude Limit for the climb phase.

The VNAV CLIMB page displays the default setting for Target Speed, Transition Altitude and Speed/Altitude Limit for the climb phase. When an altitude constraint or preselect altitude is encountered, the altitude is captured and held using an altitude hold mode.

When an altitude constraint or preselect altitude is encountered during a climb, the altitude is captured and held using an altitude hold mode. If the constraint requires the aircraft to cross the waypoint at the specified altitude, or at or below it, the specified altitude is held until the waypoint is reached. If the constraint requires crossing between two altitudes, the higher altitude is held. If the constraint is at or above the specified altitude, there is no requirement to hold an altitude. If the preselected altitude is raised while at a constraint altitude and an altitude change mode is selected, VNAV allows departure from the constraint. However, for AT, AT OR BELOW, or BETWEEN constraints, the message CHECK FPLN ALT is displayed.

The climb phase is entered whenever the flight plan target altitude and the preselect altitude are set above the altitude of the aircraft, and the autopilot is in an altitude change mode (FLC, VS, or PTCH).

During a VNAV climb, the FMS manages altitude constraints by allowing the aircraft to climb to each specified constraint altitude and hold that altitude until the constraint is cleared. If a constraint requires crossing at a specific altitude or at or below it, that altitude is held until the waypoint is reached. If the constraint is for crossing between two altitudes, the higher altitude is held. If the constraint is to cross at or above a specified altitude, no altitude hold is required. The FMS continually updates the predicted Top of Climb (TOC) and altitude intercept at constraint waypoints. If the predicted intercept violates the constraint, an UNABLE NEXT ALT message is displayed, ALT is crossed out on the PDF, and a MSG flashes on the PFD. When within capture distance, VNAV automatically sequences to VALTS or VALTV until the climb resumes. If the preselected altitude is raised while at a constraint altitude and above the flight plan target, VNAV allows departure from the constraint altitude, but may display CHECK FPLN ALT if it's an AT, AT OR BELOW, or BETWEEN constraint. If the preselect altitude is not raised sufficiently before reaching a constraint, a CHECK PRESELECTOR message is displayed.
Target Speed, Transition Altitude and Speed/Altitude Limit

altitude constraint that shows in amber indicates any one of the conditions that follow: The current rate of climb or descent is not sufficient to meet the specified flight plan altitude constraints; All climb altitude constraints do not occur before all descent altitude constraints (except for the missed approach procedure); A climb altitude constraint is lower than the climb altitude constraint that comes before it; A descent altitude constraint is higher than the descent altitude constraint that comes before it; An altitude constraint is higher than the Cruise Altitude (CRZ ALT) that was defined on the PERF INIT page.

If the predicted altitude intercept at the constraint waypoint violates the altitude constraint, amber UNABLE NEXT ALT message is displayed on the CDU, the flight mode annunciator ALT is crossed out on the PDF, and an amber MSG flashes on the PFD.

Responses: utoflight System controls aircraft pitch, roll and thrust.

The Autoflight System controls aircraft pitch, roll, and thrust via the pitch servo, roll servo, and AT servo. The system is managed and controlled by the Flight Control Panel (FCP) and other controllers on the control wheel and thrust lever. The A/T DISC Pushbutton on the thrust lever disengages the Autothrottle. The TOGA Pushbutton on the thrust lever can engage or change vertical and lateral modes to TO Mode or GA Mode.

When the A/T DISC Pushbutton is pressed:
- If AT is engaged, AT is disengaged, an AUTOTHROTTLE DISENGAGE aural alert activates, and AT flashes in the FMA then disappears.
- If AT was automatically disengaged, pressing the button cancels the AUTOTHROTTLE DISENGAGE aural alert.

When the TOGA Pushbutton is pressed:
- On the ground: If speed is less than 60 kt, vertical and lateral modes change to TO Mode. If speed is more than 60 kt, they change to GA Mode.
- In flight (if vertical and lateral modes are not TO Mode): Vertical and lateral modes change to GA Mode, the thrust mode changes to GA Mode. If AP is engaged, it is disengaged. If AT is disengaged, it is activated automatically.
- If vertical and lateral modes are TO Mode: The thrust mode changes from FLEX to TO thrust mode.
The pitch servo controls aircraft pitch commands.

ltitude Select (ALTS) Mode captures a preselected barometric altitude. This mode is controlled by the Autoflight System which utilizes the pitch servo to manage aircraft attitude according to guidance commands.

FLC Mode (Flight Level Change) holds airspeed or Mach number during climb or descent. VNAV Mode automatically selects vertical modes such as ALTS, ALT, VS, FLC, Path, or Glidepath based on FMS commands.
Descend in accordance with the glideslope signal or the FMS command.

The Overspeed and Underspeed Protection modes maintain airspeed within upper and lower limits by issuing pitch and thrust commands. In overspeed conditions, the system enters OSPD mode, generating pitch commands to reduce airspeed below Vmo/Mmo. Upon exiting OSPD mode, FLC mode engages automatically, and AT enters CLB or IDLE Thrust Mode.

The descent phase starts from Top of Descent (TOD) and continue to descent point.

The VNAV DESCENT page provides vertical information from the aircraft's current position and altitude to the next descent waypoint and descent limit altitude. It shows the waypoint identifier and associated descent constraint, and the Vertical Path Angle (VPA) to the descent constraint and the Vertical Speed Required (VSR) to reach it.

The DESCENT INFO page provides the crew with vertical information from the aircraft's current position and altitude to the next descent waypoint and descent limit altitude. The "PPOS WPT/ALT PPOS VPA/VSR" data row shows the Vertical Path Angle (VPA) in degrees to the descent constraint and the Vertical Speed Required (VSR) to reach the descent constraint. The VSR is computed based on vertical distance to the constraint, ground distance to the waypoint, and the current ground speed. The VPA is computed based on the PPOS VSR divided by the current ground speed, multiplied by a constant of 57.3° /rad.
the altitude will be captured and keep altitude hold mode.
The descent phase is entered when the target altitude and the preselect altitude in the flight plan is set below the current altitude of the aircraft.

The FMS can descend to specified constraint altitudes and hold them until the aircraft reaches the planned Top of Descent (TOD) to the next altitude constraint. If the altitude constraint requires crossing at or above a specified altitude, the aircraft holds that altitude until reaching the waypoint. If the constraint requires crossing between two altitudes, the lower altitude is held. If the constraint is at or below a specified altitude, no altitude is held during descent. Vertical Modes:
- Pitch (PTCH) Mode: Hold preselected pitch angle.
- Altitude Select (ALTS) Mode: Capture preselected barometric altitude.

- Vertical Speed Mode (VS): Hold preselected vertical speed.
- Flight Level Change (FLC) Mode: Hold airspeed or Mach number during climb or descent.
- Vertical Navigation (VNAV) Mode: FMS automatically selects ALTS, ALT, VS, FLC, Path, or Glidepath.
- Approach (APPR) Mode - Glideslope (GS) Mode: Descend in accordance with the glideslope signal or FMS command.
- Takeoff (TO) Mode - Vertical: Guidance based on takeoff target speed.
- Go-around (GA) Mode - Vertical: Guidance based on go-around target speed.
- Overspeed (OSPD) Mode: Hold fixed indicated airspeed or Mach number.
- Underspeed (USPD) Mode: Hold fixed indicated airspeed or Mach number.
- Windshear Escape Mode (WS): Hold specified pitch angle and airspeed.

Lateral Modes:
- Roll (ROLL) Mode: Hold the aircraft heading or bank angle.
- 1/2 Bank (1/2 BANK) Mode: Reduce the bank angle limit to ± 12.5°.
- Heading Select (HDG) Mode: Hold preselected heading.
- Lateral Navigation Mode (LNAV): Fly in accordance with navigation sources (FMS, LOC, VOR) during en route flight.
- APPR Mode - Lateral: Fly in accordance with navigation sources (FMS, LOC, VOR) during approach.

The Pitch (PTCH) Mode is the basic vertical mode of the Autoflight System, where the Flight Guidance (FG) generates commands to maintain the aircraft's pitch angle at the moment of mode selection. It is activated automatically when the Autoflight System is energized and the Flight Director (FD) is engaged for the first time, or if no other vertical modes are selected. Engaging the Autopilot (AP) when both FDs are disengaged also activates PTCH Mode. Turning the PITCH/VS Wheel in any of the listed modes (ALTS, ALT, FLC, GA, PATH Angle, GP, OSPD) will activate PTCH Mode. The pitch reference synchronizes to the current pitch angle when PTCH Mode is activated, the SYNC Pushbutton is pressed, AP is engaged with no other vertical modes selected, the FD is engaged after AP and both FDs are disengaged, or the FG coupled side changes and PTCH Mode is activated.

The Altitude Select (ALTS) Mode is a vertical mode that captures a preselected barometric altitude. It is activated during altitude capture when a new attitude is selected or the current altitude is being maintained.

When an overspeed condition occurs (Mach number > Mmo + 0.01 or airspeed > Vmo + 5 kt), Overspeed (OSPD) Mode automatically activates to generate pitch commands to reduce airspeed below Vmo/Mmo, with a speed reference of Mmo - 0.02 or Vmo - 10 kt. When a significant low speed occurs, Underspeed (USPD) Mode automatically activates to generate pitch commands to increase airspeed above Vman or Mman. In both OSPD and USPD modes, the SPEED Knob is inhibited and Autothrottle (AT) is armed. AP does not disengage in either mode but reverts to armed status (white ARM on FMA). Vertical and Lateral Modes are engaged and disengaged through pushbuttons on the Flight Control Panel (FCP). When a mode is selected, incompatible modes are automatically deselected. AT Modes are integrated with vertical/lateral modes and the FMS, automatically selected based on active vertical modes. During all flight operations, it is critical for the pilot to recognize and understand the active and armed Modes of the Autoflight System.
Incompatible Modes will be automatically deselected.

When the Autoflight System is energized and the FD is engaged for the first time, PTCH Mode is activated automatically. If no other vertical modes are selected, PTCH is the default vertical mode. If a lateral mode is activated before a vertical mode is selected, PTCH is the default. Engaging the AP when both FDs are disengaged also activates PTCH Mode. Incompatible vertical modes are automatically deselected when PTCH Mode is selected.

The ALTS Mode is always armed except when the ALT Mode, the GS Mode, or the GA Mode is active. The ALTS Mode is engaged when selected by pressing the appropriate button on the FCP. The ALTS Mode is disengaged when the ALT, GS, or GA Mode becomes active, or when the ALT knob on the FCP is rotated, which inhibits ALTS to prevent altitude capture during preselected altitude changes.

The Vertical Speed (VS) Mode is engaged and disengaged through the related pushbuttons on the Flight Control Panel (FCP). It can also be deselected by selecting other vertical modes or capturing other vertical modes.

When VNAV is active, the FMS can automatically select vertical modes such as ALTS, ALT, VS, or FLC based on flight plan constraints and provide corresponding altitude and speed references. In Path Mode, the FG tracks the FMS vertical path, and in Glidepath Mode, it tracks the FMS glidepath. VNAV also allows the Autoflight System to follow FMS vertical profile constraints and provides references for these modes.
In the APPR Mode, the GS Mode generates commands to capture or track the selected glideslope, and the AT controls airspeed.

The OSPD Mode is automatically activated when overspeed occurs (Mach number > Mmo + 0.01 or airspeed > Vmo + 5 kt), unless ALTS, ALT, or GS Mode are active. The system generates pitch commands to reduce airspeed below Vmo/Mmo, with a speed reference of Mmo - 0.02 or Vmo - 10 kt. The SPEED Knob is inhibited, and AT is armed. The system returns to FLC Mode when airspeed is below the limit.

The Underspeed (USPD) Mode is a protection mode that automatically activates if a significant low-speed condition occurs, preventing stall. It generates pitch commands to increase airspeed above Vman or Mman. Once airspeed is above Vman/Mman, USPD deactivates automatically, setting the airspeed reference to Vman + 5 kt/Mman +0.01. The vertical mode then switches to FLC Mode. USPD mode is inhibited below 1000 ft after takeoff, after GS capture during ILS approach, and is not activated in ALT or ALTS Mode during cruise. When USPD mode is active, the SPEED Knob is inhibited, and all vertical modes except ALTS, ALT, TO, and GA are inhibited. The AT is armed when USPD is active.

Responses: VNAV CLIMB
VNAV CLIMB

When an altitude constraint or preselect altitude is encountered during a climb, VNAV captures and holds the altitude using an altitude hold mode. The FLC mode controls pitch to maintain the commanded IAS or Mach speed, while the altitude hold mode controls pitch to maintain the commanded altitude.

When an altitude constraint or preselect altitude is encountered during a climb, the altitude is captured and held using an altitude hold mode. The FLC mode controls pitch to maintain the commanded Indicated Airspeed (IAS) or Mach speed. The altitude hold mode controls pitch to maintain the commanded altitude. When the aircraft is within capture distance of the constraint altitude, the VNAV mode automatically sequences to VALTS or VALTV, and remains in VALTS, VALTV, or VALT until a climb is resumed.

The climb phase is entered whenever the flight plan target altitude and the preselect altitude are set above the altitude of the aircraft, and the autopilot is in an altitude change mode (FLC, VS, or PTCH).

VNAV allows the aircraft to climb to each constraint altitude and hold that altitude until the constraint is cleared. If the altitude constraint requires crossing at a specific altitude or at or below, the specified altitude is held until the waypoint is reached. If it requires crossing between two altitudes, the higher altitude is held. If it requires crossing at or above, there is no requirement to hold altitude. When approaching a constraint, VNAV updates the predicted Top of Climb and altitude intercept. If the intercept violates the constraint, an amber UNABLE NEXT ALT message is displayed, ALT on the PFD is crossed out, and a flashing amber MSG appears. If the preselected altitude is raised while at a constraint altitude (AT, AT OR BELOW, or BETWEEN), and an altitude change mode is selected, VNAV allows departure, but displays CHECK FPLN ALT. When within capture distance, VNAV sequences to VALTS or VALTV and remains in altitude hold until the climb resumes. If the preselect altitude is not raised before reaching the constraint, CHECK PRESELECTOR is displayed. If raised before the constraint, VNAV sequences to VFLC and resumes the climb after crossing the waypoint.
VNAV climb data displayed for waypoints during the climb phase includes altitude constraints and speed limits.

If the predicted altitude intercept at the constraint waypoint violates the altitude constraint, amber UNABLE NEXT ALT message is displayed on the CDU, the flight mode annunciator ALT is crossed out on the PDF, and an amber MSG flashes on the PFD.

Responses: The Autoflight System controls aircraft pitch, roll and thrust.

The Autoflight System controls aircraft pitch, roll, and thrust via the pitch servo, roll servo, and AT servo. The vertical, lateral, and AT modes are displayed on the FMA at the top of the PFD. The Autopilot (AP) has the functions of auto pitch trim. When the AP is engaged, the automatic pitch trim function activates. The automatic pitch trim function deactivates when the AP is disengaged, if faults are detected, or if the SYNC Pushbutton is pressed while the AP is engaged. The AT Modes are integrated with the vertical/lateral modes and the flight management system. The A/T DISC Pushbutton on the thrust lever disengages the AT if it is engaged. The TOGA Pushbutton on the thrust lever can engage GA Mode or TO Mode depending on the flight conditions.
The pitch servo, roll servo, and AT servo control the aircraft's pitch, roll, and thrust, respectively. The vertical Mode, lateral Mode, and AT Mode are displayed on the FMA at the top of the PFD.

The Pitch (PTCH) Mode is the basic vertical mode of the Autoflight System where the Flight Guidance (FG) generates commands to hold the actual aircraft pitch angle at the time of mode selection. It can be activated automatically when the Autoflight System is energized and the Flight Director (FD) is engaged for the first time, or if no other vertical modes are selected. If a lateral mode is activated before a vertical mode, PTCH is the default. Engaging the Autopilot (AP) when both FDs are disengaged also activates PTCH mode. The pitch angle reference can be changed using the PITCH/VS Wheel, with a range of -15° to 20°. The PTCH Mode can be activated by turning the PITCH/VS Wheel in other modes such as Altitude Select (ALTS), Altitude Hold (ALT), Flight Level Change (FLC), Go-around (GA), PATH Angle, Glidepath (GP), and Overspeed (OSPD). The pitch reference synchronizes to the current pitch angle when PTCH Mode is activated, the SYNC Pushbutton is pressed, or under certain AP engagement and FD conditions. In PTCH Mode, the Autothrottle (AT) controls airspeed.
Capture preselected barometric altitude.

In the climb phase, VNAV provides speed and altitude targets consistent with climb constraints and speed limits, and it uses FLC mode (VFLC on PFD) for automatic mode sequencing. The FLC mode controls pitch to maintain the commanded Indicated Airspeed (IAS) or Mach speed.

The Glidepath (GP) Mode descends in accordance with the glideslope signal or the FMS command. The Vertical Navigation (VNAV) Mode automatically selects the Mode of ALTS, ALT, VS, FLC, Path or Glidepath.

The Overspeed (OSPD) Mode generates pitch commands to lower airspeed below Vmo/Mmo. The Underspeed (USPD) Mode sends pitch commands to increase airspeed over Vman/Mman. Both modes are engaged when the AP and AT are engaged and airspeed limits are exceeded.

**Vertical Modes:**
*   **Pitch (PTCH) Mode:** Holds a preselected pitch angle.
*   **Altitude Select (ALTS) Mode:** Captures a preselected barometric altitude.
*   **Altitude Hold (ALT) Mode:** Holds the current barometric altitude.
*   **Vertical Speed (VS) Mode:** Holds a preselected vertical speed.
*   **Flight Level Change (FLC) Mode:** Holds an airspeed or Mach number during climb or descent.
*   **Vertical Navigation (VNAV) Mode:** The FMS automatically selects modes like ALTS, ALT, VS, FLC, Path, or Glidepath.
*   **Approach (APPR) Mode - Glideslope (GS) Mode:** Descends according to the glideslope signal or FMS command.
*   **Takeoff (TO) Mode - Vertical:** Provides vertical guidance based on a takeoff target speed.
*   **Go-around (GA) Mode - Vertical:** Provides vertical guidance based on a go-around target speed.
*   **Overspeed (OSPD) Mode:** Holds a fixed indicated airspeed or Mach number.
*   **Underspeed (USPD) Mode:** Holds a fixed indicated airspeed or Mach number.
*   **Windshear Escape Mode (WS):** Holds a specified pitch angle and airspeed.

**Lateral Modes:**
*   **Roll (ROLL) Mode:** Holds the aircraft heading or bank angle.
*   **1/2 Bank (1/2 BANK) Mode:** Reduces the bank angle limit to ±12.5°.
*   **Heading Select (HDG) Mode:** Holds a preselected heading.
*   **Lateral Navigation (LNAV) Mode:** Flies in accordance with navigation sources (FMS, LOC, VOR) during en route flight.
*   **Approach (APPR) Mode - Lateral:** Flies in accordance with navigation sources (FMS, LOC, VOR) during approach.
*   **Takeoff (TO) Mode - Lateral:** Holds the aircraft's heading reference.
*   **Go-around (GA) Mode - Lateral:** Holds the aircraft's current heading.

**Autothrottle (AT) Modes:**
*   **Thrust Control Mode:** Manages engine thrust.
*   **Speed Control Mode:** Manages aircraft speed.
*   **Underspeed and Overspeed Protection Mode:** Provides protection against underspeed and overspeed conditions.

The FMS allows for several methods of modifying a flight plan, including:

**Waypoint Creation:**

*   **Insert/Add a Waypoint:** This general operation allows adding waypoints from the navigation database to the flight plan.
*   **Create a Flyover Waypoint:** This is done by adding a "/0" suffix to a waypoint identifier. The aircraft must fly over this waypoint before sequencing to the next.
*   **Create Pilot-Defined Waypoints:**
    *   **Along-Track Offset (ATO) Waypoint / Position/Distance (PD) Waypoint:** Creates a waypoint at a specific distance before or after an existing waypoint along the flight path.
    *   **General Pilot-Defined Waypoints:** Allows the creation of unique waypoints that can be stored with or without a name. Up to 100 can be stored in the FMS, with a maximum of 50 in a single flight plan.
*   **Insert/Add a Direct Waypoint:** Adds a "TO" waypoint to the flight plan on the ACT/MOD FPLN page.
*   **Select Pilot-Defined Waypoints:** Retrieves stored waypoints from the PILOT WPT LIST and inserts them into the flight plan.
*   **Change a FIX INFO to a Waypoint:** Allows converting certain fixes from the FIX INFO page into usable waypoints for the flight plan.

**Waypoint Deletion:**

*   **Delete a Discontinuity (FROM Waypoint Edit):** While not a direct deletion of a waypoint *from* the flight plan in the traditional sense, selecting a down-track waypoint as the new FROM waypoint deletes all waypoints between the current FROM waypoint and the new FROM waypoint. The Direct-From waypoint is also deleted when transferred. The context doesn't explicitly describe a general "delete waypoint" function for arbitrary waypoints within the flight plan.

The CDUs are used to control the FMS and its functions, including flight plan creation, editing, and management, as well as performance calculations and navigation selections.

The FMS provides data to support the display of north-up and heading oriented map formats. The CDU displays alert messages such as FMS DR, CHK POS, FMS-FMS DISAGREE, or GNSS-FMS DISAGREE. Additionally, for localizer-based approaches, messages like LOC WILL BE TUNED or CHECK LOC TUNING can be displayed on the CDU.

The scratchpad entry line is used to display the position as a radial and distance from the selected Navigation Aid (NAVAID) when updating the FMS position. It is also used to enter the NAVAID identifier if it is not displayed correctly. Additionally, it is where fix coordinates are entered for LAT CROSS and LON CROSS fixes, and where the message NO INTERSECTION appears if the coordinates do not intersect the flight plan.

The scratchpad line on the CDU is used for entering information, such as waypoint identifiers, radial and distance from a selected Navigation Aid (NAVAID) for position updates, or coordinates for crossing latitude/longitude fixes.

Responses: Normal Brake System, Park/emergency brake system, Brake temperature monitoring system

The wheel brake system includes the Normal Brake System (Manual and Autobrake), Park/emergency brake system (Emergency brake and Parking brake), and Brake temperature monitoring system. The system is electrically controlled and hydraulically actuated. No.1 hydraulic system charges the Inboard Brake Accumulator and supplies pressure to the inboard wheel brakes. No.2 hydraulic system charges the Outboard Brake Accumulator and supplies pressure to the outboard wheel brakes. Brake accumulators provide pressure if a hydraulic system fails, and can supply pressure for six emergency brake applications with all hydraulic systems failed. Fusible plugs on main wheels prevent tire bursting, and tire overpressure relief valves on nose and main wheels prevent blowout. Wear pins indicate brake wear, and temperature sensors send data to the Brake Control Unit (BCU), displayed on EICAS.
Brake Control Unit (BCU)

No.1 hydraulic system supplies pressure to the inboard wheel brakes, while No.2 hydraulic system supplies pressure to the outboard wheel brakes. Brake accumulators charge from their respective hydraulic systems and supply pressure to the brakes if the hydraulic systems fail, providing six full brake applications for the emergency brake.

The TCAS system detects aircraft equipped with transponders in its vicinity, displays potential and predicted collision targets, and issues vertical maneuvering indications to avoid conflicts. It operates independently of ground-based ATC and has a detection range of up to 30-40 NM laterally and 9900 ft vertically. TCAS constantly interrogates other aircraft transponders to determine their relative bearing, range, closure rate, and relative altitude. It then computes intruder trajectories, Closest Point of Approach (CPA), and estimated time to CPA, triggering alerts when a collision threat is present. TCAS optimizes vertical orders to ensure sufficient trajectory separation and a variable minimal vertical speed.

Responses: Normal Brake System, Park/emergency brake system, Brake temperature monitoring system

The wheel brake system includes the Normal Brake System, Park/emergency brake system, and Brake temperature monitoring system. The normal brake system has manual and autobrake modes. The park/emergency brake system has emergency and parking brake modes. The brake system is electrically controlled and hydraulically actuated by the Brake Control Unit (BCU). No. 1 hydraulic system supplies pressure to the inboard wheel brakes, and No. 2 hydraulic system supplies pressure to the outboard wheel brakes, with check valves preventing backflow. Brake accumulators supply pressure if hydraulic systems fail, providing six emergency brake applications. The main wheels have fusible plugs and tire overpressure relief valves, and wear pins indicate brake wear. Temperature sensors on each brake send information to the BCU for display on EICAS.

No.1 hydraulic system charges the Inboard Brake Accumulator and supplies pressure to the inboard wheel brakes. No.2 hydraulic system charges the Outboard Brake Accumulator and supplies pressure to the outboard wheel brakes.

Responses: MFD menus are controlled by the UPR MENU, LWR MENU and ESC buttons and the MENU ADV/DATA knob on the CCP.

The MFD display is divided into an upper and a lower window. The UPR MENU button selects the MFD menu for the upper window. The LWR MENU button selects the MFD menu for the lower window. The ESC button steps out of selected menus. The MENU ADV/DATA knob moves the focus indicator within a menu and selects options.

Menu items are changed using the selection box method. Navigation within menus is done by turning the MENU ADV/DATA knob to move the focus indicator up and down or between options, and the PUSH SELECT button to select an option.

Pressing or repeatedly pressing the ESC button will remove the MFD Menu no matter at which level. The upper and lower menus are mutually exclusive with the last button pressed clearing any open menu in the opposite window and displaying the menu associated with the button pressed. If a MFD menu is displayed and one of the following Cursor Control Panel (CCP) buttons is selected, then the menu will be removed (no menu): TFC Button, TERR Button, WX Button, Memory 1, 2 or 3 Button, MENU ADV/DATA Knob, or Any Synoptic Page Button. The menu will be automatically removed after 10 s without menu operation.

Responses: PACKs, mixing manifold, recirculation fa

Bleed air enters the PACKs, where it is cooled and its pressure adjusted. The air from the PACKs is then delivered to the mixing manifold, where it is combined with recirculated cabin air before being distributed to the cabin.

The integrated air system controller 1 controls the left PACK and the integrated air system controller 2 controls the right PACK. The mixing manifold combines air from the PACKs and recirculation fans.

When one PACK fails, the other PACK provides normal system operations, but limited to an altitude of 31000 ft. When both PACKs fail, the flight altitude is limited to below 10000 ft and CAB ΔP is less than 1 psi.
When both PACKs fail, the flight altitude is limited to below 10000 ft and CAB ΔP is less than 1 psi.

The priorities of the Stall Protection System (SPS) modes reduce in the sequence: Flap/Slat System Fail Advance Mode, ADVANCE ON Mode, Ice Advance Mode 3, Ice Advance Mode 2, Ice Advance Mode 1, and normal Mode. The AOA of stall alert and stick pusher is the same between Ice Advance Mode 1 and Ice Advance Mode 2. It's also the same between Ice Advance Mode 3 and ADVANCE ON Mode. Bleed air enters the primary heat exchanger through the Flow Control Valve to decrease temperature and pressure. It is then compressed by the air cycle machine's compressor, further cooled in the main heat exchanger, and then reheated/condensed. landing mode and takeoff mod
The initiation of brake application during landing.
The initiation of brake application during a rejected takeoff.
The autobrake system has two operating modes: landing mode, used for initiating brake application during landing, and takeoff mode, used for initiating brake application during a rejected takeoff.
ming, Enable and Applicatio
The autobrake is armed when the autobrake is set (LO, MED and HI), the Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals indicate that the aircraft is in flight, and the brake system does not detect a fault.

The autobrake is disarmed after arming if the brake system detects a fault, the AUTOBRAKE Selector is set to a position other than RTO (for takeoff mode) or OFF (for landing mode), an "arm disagree" occurs between the two channels of the Brake Control Unit (BCU), or the Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals disagree. For takeoff mode specifically, it is also disarmed if one or more WOW signals indicate the aircraft is in flight.

**For Takeoff Mode:**
* All Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals indicate that the aircraft is on the ground.
* The wheel speed is below 55 kt.
* The brake system does not detect a fault.

**For Landing Mode:**
* The Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals indicate that the aircraft is in flight.
* The brake system does not detect a fault.

The autobrake system operates when two thrust levers are in IDLE or reverser position, and the AUTOBRAKE Selector is in RTO. For landing mode, braking starts automatically when autobrake is activated, both thrust levers are at IDLE or in the reverser position, and these conditions are met for 3 seconds.

The autobrake system disarms during application if the brake system detects a fault, the AUTOBRAKE Selector is not in RTO (for takeoff mode) or is set to OFF or RTO (for landing mode), brake pedal application is 25% greater than total application available, one or more Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals indicate the aircraft is in flight, any thrust lever is pushed forward to a position greater than IDLE, or the ground spoilers are retracted from the extended position (only for landing mode).
ming: All Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals indicate that the aircraft is on the ground. The wheel speed is below 55 kt. The brake system does not detect a fault. Enable: The wheel speed is above 60 kt.
ll Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals indicate that the aircraft is on the ground, the wheel speed is below 55 kt, and the brake system does not detect a fault.

- One or more Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals indicate the aircraft is in flight (for takeoff mode) or the WOW signals disagree (for both modes).
- An "arm disagree" between the two channels of the Brake Control Unit (BCU) occurs.

**Landing Mode Enabled Status Disarm Conditions:**
* The same conditions causing the autobrake to disarm after arming occurs (brake system detects a fault, AUTOBRAKE Selector is set to OFF, "arm disagree" between BCU channels, or WOW signals disagree).

The key functionalities of TCAS are: detecting aircraft with transponders in its vicinity, displaying potential and predicted collision targets, and issuing vertical maneuvering indications to avoid conflicts. It is independent of ground-based ATC and has a limited detection range.

TCAS constantly interrogates other aircraft ATC transponders. Depending on the replies, TCAS determines for each intruder its relative bearing, range and closure rate, and relative altitude. Then, TCAS computes the intruder trajectory, the Closest Point of Approach (CPA) and the estimated time (TAU) to reach the CPA.

Responses: The two CDUs provide the basic control and display of the FMS for the flight crew. They also provide display and control of datalink function, and both CDUs can display and control the datalink pages.

The CDUs provide the basic control and display of the FMS, including computed navigation data, datalink function pages, and display menu pages such as MAP DISPLAY and TEXT DISPLAY. They can also display specific pages like TAKEOFF REF, APPROACH REF, ACT FPLN PROGRESS, NAV STATUS, POSITION SUMMARY, POS REPORT, SEC FPLN, VOR STATUS, GNSS STATUS, and IRS STATUS.

The Line Select Keys (LSKs) on the CDUs execute related functions. They can be used to copy or transfer data between the scratchpad and a line, or to select a mode of operation or function related to the display page. The DSPL MENU key, when pressed, displays the MAP DISPLAY page or TEXT DISPLAY page on the CDU. On the TEXT DISPLAY page, LSKs can be pressed to select functions such as TO+APPR REF, FPLN PROG, NAV STATUS, POS SUMMARY, POS REPORT, SEC FPLN, VOR STATUS, and LRN STATUS, which then display corresponding information on the MFD.

There are six LSKs on each side of the CDU display screen, identified as L1-L6 and R1-R6. Pressing an LSK executes the related function, which can include copying data to or from the scratchpad, or selecting a mode of operation or function related to the displayed page.

The main components of the air conditioning system are the two PACKs and the mixing manifold. Bleed air enters the PACKs, where its temperature and pressure are adjusted through a process involving a primary heat exchanger, compressor, main heat exchanger, reheater/condenser, and water separator. The processed air is then delivered to the mixing manifold.
The Integrated Air System Controllers (IASCs) control the PACKs. The mixing manifold combines air from the PACKs and the recirculation fans.
When one PACK fails, the other PACK provides normal system operations, but limited to an altitude of 31000 ft.

When both PACKs fail, the flight altitude is limited to below 10000 ft and CAB ΔP is less than 1 psi. Sufficient fresh air can be provided to the cockpit and cabin through the emergency RAM air valve.

When both PACKs fail, the outside air flows through the electrically controlled emergency RAM air valve to provide adequate fresh air in the cockpit and cabin, provided the flight altitude is below 10000 ft and CAB ΔP is less than 1 psi.
When both PACKs fail, and the flight altitude is limited to below 10000 ft and CAB ΔP is less than 1 psi.
The emergency RAM air valve is connected to the mixing manifold.
The mixing manifold combines air from the PACKs and the recirculation fans and is also connected to the Emergency RAM air valve and low pressure ground connection.

The trim air pressure regulating valve and trim air valve adjust the pressure and flow of hot bleed air from the engine or APU. This hot trim air is then mixed with the air from the mixing manifold in the air conditioning distribution duct, and then distributed to the cockpit and cabin to maintain selected temperature. Responses: Stall alert, stall protection and auto-ignition functions.
Two Angle of Attack (AOA) Sensors integrated with Stall Protection Computers (SPC), one stick pusher integrated in AP pitch servo to execute the stick pushing function, and two stick shakers.

The Stall Protection System (SPS) includes two sets of integrated AOA sensors/stall protection computers, each with a Stall Protection Computer (SPC). These two SPCs complete independent computations, and each can independently initiate stall alert, stall protection, and auto-ignition.
Stall alert, stall protection and auto-ignitio
Stall Protection System provides stall alert, stall protection and auto-ignition functions.
The Stall Protection Computer (SPC) commands the AP pitch servo motor to activate the stick pusher. Only when both SPCs generate stall pusher commands simultaneously will the stick pusher activate.
gle of Attack (AOA), FLAP angle, Airspeed/Mach number, Normal overload, side overload, Ice signal, WING A/I Switch signal, STALL ADVANCE Switch, WOW Signal.
Integrated Standby Instrument (ISI)

Stall alert, stall shaker and pusher commands are generated, as well as auto-ignition control signals. The stick-push commands are sent to the autoflight system by the IPC which controls the pitch servo to drive the elevator.

The Stall Protection Computer (SPC) generates stall alert, stall shaker, and pusher commands when the aircraft's Angle of Attack (AOA) reaches a calculated threshold. The stick pusher activates only when both SPCs generate stall pusher commands simultaneously and the AOA continues to increase beyond the stick shaker activation level.
Stall Protection System provides stall alert, stall protection and auto-ignition functions.

The Stall Protection System (SPS) has the following modes with priorities reducing in sequence: Flap/Slat System Fail Advance Mode, ADVANCE ON Mode, Ice Advance Mode 3, Ice Advance Mode 2, Ice Advance Mode 1, and Normal Mode. Compared to normal mode, the threshold values for stall alert, stall protection (stick pusher), and auto-ignition AOA are decreased in the other modes.

Compared to normal mode, the threshold value for stall alert, stall protection stick pusher and auto-ignition AOA in other modes decrease. The AOA of stall alert and stick pusher is the same between Ice Advance Mode 1 and Ice Advance Mode 2. It's also the same between Ice Advance Mode 3 and ADVANCE ON Mode. However the AOA of the former (Ice Advance Mode 1 and 2) is greater than that of the latter one (Ice Advance Mode 3 and ADVANCE ON Mode).
Ice Advance Mode 1 and 2
Ice detector on either side detects ice, Wing anti-ice system available, STALL ADVANCE Switch is released.
Ice detector on either side detects ice, Wing anti-ice system available, and STALL ADVANCE Switch is released.
Ice detector on either side detects ice, Wing Anti-Ice System fails, STALL ADVANCE Switch is released.
The ADVANCE ON Mode activates if the STALL ADVANCE Switch is pushed, and the ON light illuminates.

The Stall Protection System (SPS) enters Flap/Slat Fail Advance Mode in any of the following conditions: Flap system fails on FSECU bus, and flap configuration is not in 0. Flap system fails on FSECU bus or slat angle on both sides is not available, and flap configuration is not in 0. The slat angle difference between the two sides is 3° for 5 s, and flap configuration is not in 0.

The Stall Protection System (SPS) reverts to normal mode when the conditions that triggered the Flap/Slat Fail Advance Mode are no longer satisfied. For Ice Advance Mode 2, the system remains in this mode even if the conditions are not met, unless a higher priority mode is triggered, or the STALL ADVANCE Switch is released manually, leading to a logical judgment based on the current status. Other advance modes are not explicitly stated to revert to normal mode based on condition satisfaction, but rather through manual intervention or when re-energized after power loss.

Stall Protection System (SPS) Ice Advance Mode 2 exits when the STALL ADVANCE Switch is cycled while the flap is down and the aircraft is in level flight. The SPS ICE MODE 2 message disappears from the EICAS display. Note that this mode does not exit automatically after the WING A/I Switch is engaged.
Stall Protection System (SPS) Ice Advance Mode 2 can exit when the flap is down and aircraft is in level flight, by cycling the STALL ADVANCE Switch.
Ice Advance Mode 2 cannot exit automatically.

Manually cycling the STALL ADVANCE Switch in Ice Advance Mode 2 allows the pilot to exit this mode by returning the system to normal mode or Advance On Mode after a logical judgment based on the current status.

When the Stall Protection Computer (SPC) is powered on, the ADVANCE ON Mode (and other Advance Modes) is not affected by the aircraft's air/ground status. The SPC will remain in the Advance Mode even if the air/ground condition changes.

The stick pusher activates when the airframe AOA is less than the threshold of the stick shaker decreased by 0.8°, or normal overload is less than 0.5g (whichever occurs first). Only when both SPC's generate stall pusher commands at the same time, will the stick pusher activate.
DVANCE ON Mode activates.

Compared to normal mode, the threshold value for stall alert, stall protection stick pusher and auto-ignition AOA in other modes decrease. The Advance On Mode, drives the stall alert (stick vibration, STALL aural alert and the warning flag on the PFD).

via the outflow valv

Bleed air from the pneumatic system is adjusted by two flow control valves, and then temperature and pressure are adjusted by two PACKs. The bleed air then enters the mixing manifold to be mixed with recirculated cabin air. Hot trim air is mixed with the air from the mixing manifold in the air conditioning distribution duct, and then distributed to the cockpit and cabin.
mixing manifold
circulated air from the cabi

Part of the recirculated air is sent to the mixing manifold to mix with the fresh cold air from the PACK, and the rest is sent to the AFT cargo compartment for ventilation.
The air conditioning system is controlled and monitored by two Integrated Air System Controllers (IASCs). The PACKs adjust bleed air temperature and pressure.

The integrated air system controllers control the shutoff and overheat protection of bleed air, temperature regulation of the air conditioning system, and flow monitoring by regulating the flow control valves.
The integrated air system controllers regulate the flow control valves by controlling their shutoff and overheat protection, and by regulating flow.

If one PACK fails, the other PACK provides normal system operations, but limited to an altitude of 31000 ft. If both PACKs fail, the flight altitude is limited to below 10000 ft and CAB ΔP is less than 1 psi. When these conditions are satisfied, sufficient fresh air can be provided to the cockpit and cabin through the emergency RAM air valve. The IASCs control the PACKs.

ming, Enable and Applicatio

When the AUTOBRAKE Selector is set to RTO, and all Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals indicate that the aircraft is on the ground, the wheel speed is below 55 kt, and the brake system does not detect a fault.

The autobrake is disarmed after arming in any of the following conditions: The brake system detects a fault. The AUTOBRAKE Selector is set to a position other than RTO. One or more Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals indicate that the aircraft is in flight. An "arm disagree" between the two channels of the Brake Control Unit (BCU). The Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals received by the wheel brake system disagree.

The autobrake system has two operating modes: landing mode and takeoff mode.
Landing Mode:
1. Arming: When the autobrake is set (LO, MED and HI), it is armed if the aircraft is in flight and the brake system does not detect a fault.
2. Enable: The autobrake landing mode is enabled if the aircraft is on the ground and the wheel speed is above 60 kt.
3. Application: Braking starts automatically at the selected deceleration rate when the autobrake is activated, both thrust levers are at IDLE or in the reverser position, and these conditions are met for 3 s.

Takeoff Mode:
1. Arming: When the AUTOBRAKE Selector is set to RTO, the autobrake takeoff mode is armed if all Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals indicate the aircraft is on the ground, the wheel speed is below 55 kt, and the brake system does not detect a fault.
2. Enable: The autobrake is enabled when the wheel speed is above 60 kt.
3. Application: The autobrake system operates if the AUTOBRAKE Selector is in RTO and two thrust levers are in IDLE or reverser position.

The autobrake is disarmed after being enabled if:
- The AUTOBRAKE Selector is set to a position other than RTO.
- One or more Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals indicate that the aircraft is in flight.
- The brake system detects a fault.
- An "arm disagree" between the two channels of the Brake Control Unit (BCU).

The autobrake system operates in the application phase when the following conditions are met: Two thrust levers are in IDLE or reverser position. The AUTOBRAKE Selector is in RTO for takeoff mode. For landing mode, the autobrake is activated, both thrust levers are at IDLE or in the reverser position, and the conditions for activation have been met for 3 seconds.

During autobrake application, the autobrake will disarm in any of the following conditions:
- The wheel brake system detects a fault.
- The AUTOBRAKE Selector is not in RTO.
- The application of any brake pedal is 25 % greater than the total application available and lasts for 1 s.
- One or more Weight-on-Wheels (WOW) signals indicate that the aircraft is in flight.
- Any thrust lever is pushed forward to a position greater than IDLE.
- The ground spoilers are retracted from the extended position.

TCAS has the following functions:
- Detects any aircraft, equipped with transponders, flying in its vicinity.
- Displays potential and predicted collision targets.
- Issues vertical maneuvering indications to avoid conflict.
TCAS is independent of the ground-based ATC.

When the relative position of the intruder presents a collision threat, TCAS computes the intruder trajectory, the Closest Point of Approach (CPA) and the estimated time (TAU) to reach the CPA, and then triggers aural and visual alerts. TCAS optimizes vertical orders to ensure sufficient trajectory separation and a variable minimal vertical speed considering all intruders.

- Proximate traffic: No collision threat, traffic in the vicinity. Displayed as an unfilled cyan diamond.
- Traffic Advisory (TA): Potential collision threat. Displayed as a filled amber circle with aural messages.
- Resolution Advisory (RA): Real collision threat. Displayed as a filled red box with aural messages and vertical maneuvering indications on the PFD to ensure trajectory separation.
- Preventive Resolution Advisory (PRA): Warns the pilot to avoid deviation from the present vertical flight path.
- Corrective Resolution Advisory (CRA): Warns the pilot to take actions (such as climb or descent) to avoid threat aggravation.
Proximate traffic is identified as traffic in the vicinity, closer than 6 NM laterally and ± 1200 ft vertically, and is displayed as a filled cyan diamond on the PFD/MFD.
Traffic Advisory (TA) informs the pilot of proximate traffic which does not constitute a threat at present but may become a threat when the conditions change. Its associated TAU is about 40 seconds.
Traffic Advisory (TA) is displayed as a filled amber circle on the PFD/MFD. It also triggers the aural message "TRAFFIC, TRAFFIC".
Resolution Advisory (RA) is a real collision threat, with an associated TAU of about 25 seconds.

Resolution Advisories (RAs) are displayed as a filled red box on the PFD/MFD. They trigger aural messages and vertical maneuvering orders displayed on the vertical speed scale of the PFD to either maintain the current V/S (preventive resolution advisory - PRA), modify the V/S (corrective resolution advisory - CRA), or ensure vertical speed is outside the red area ("MONITOR VERTICAL SPEED"). Specific aural alerts include "CLIMB, CLIMB", "DESCEND, DESCEND", "LEVEL OFF, LEVEL OFF", "CLIMB, CLIMB NOW", "DESCEND, DESCEND NOW", "INCREASE CLIMB", "INCREASE DESCENT", "MAINTAIN VERTICAL SPEED", and "MAINTAIN VERTICAL SPEED, CROSSING MAINTAIN". If the conflict is cleared, "CLEAR OF CONFLICT" is announced.
Preventive Resolution Advisory (PRA) and Corrective Resolution Advisory (CRA)

The different classifications of intruders in TCAS are: Proximate traffic, Traffic Advisory (TA), Resolution Advisory (RA), and Other Traffic.

"Other Traffic" is identified as traffic with no collision threat, and its optional position can be displayed within the surveillance envelope. It is displayed on the PFD/MFD as an unfilled cyan diamond.

TCAS RAs are inhibited below 1100 ft AGL during climb or below 900 ft AGL during descend. The CRS 1 Knob and CRS 2 Knob on the Flight Control Panel (FCP) can be used to manually select the course. When the FMS is the active navigation source, the course is set automatically by the FMS and the related CRS Knob is inoperative.

The LNAV Mode can be deselected by selecting other lateral modes.

The LNAV Mode is selected by pressing the LNAV Button on the Flight Control Panel (FCP). It is activated when the aircraft is on an intercept heading to the selected course, and the HDG Mode is deselected. Activation occurs without delay if VOR/LOC deviation is minimum at selection. The LNAV Mode generates commands to track the selected navigation source (FMS/LOC/VOR). If the aircraft is not on an intercept heading or the source is invalid, LNAV is armed, and the FG operates in HDG Mode. The system operates in Dead Reckoning Mode during VOR station overfly. LNAV can be deselected by changing the active navigation source, its frequency, the FG coupled side, or by selecting other lateral modes. When FMS is the active source, the course is set automatically by the FMS, making the CRS Knob inoperative.

Responses: MFD menus are controlled by the UPR MENU, LWR MENU and ESC buttons and the MENU ADV/DATA knob on the CCP.

The UPR MENU button selects the MFD menu for the upper window. The LWR MENU button selects the MFD menu for the lower window. The ESC button steps out of a selected menu. The MENU ADV/DATA knob moves the focus indicator within a menu and selects options.

To navigate and select items within MFD menus, use the MENU ADV/DATA knob on the CCP. The outer ring (MENU ADV Knob) moves the focus indicator up and down within the menu. The inner knob (DATA Knob) moves the focus indicator between options or allows for input of control values. The PUSH SELECT button in the middle of the knob is used to select an option once it is highlighted.

MFD menus can be exited or removed by pressing or repeatedly pressing the ESC button, or by the menu automatically removing after 10 seconds of inactivity. 1. Set the REFUEL SELECTION Switch to AUTO.
2. Use the INCR/DECRT Switch to set the target refuel quantity.
3. Manually open the Refuel Shutoff Valve to start refueling.

8. If the fuel imbalance reaches 400 kg (882 lb) during refueling, the FQC will close the refuel shutoff valve in the tank with the higher quantity. When fuel quantities are balanced, both refuel shutoff valves are opened to complete refueling simultaneously.
9. Refueling is completed when the combined total equals the preselected value.

The Fuel Quantity Computer (FQC) balances fuel quantities by shutting off the refuel shutoff valve in the tank with the higher quantity when an imbalance of more than 400 kg (882 lb) occurs, and then reopening both valves when the tanks are balanced to refuel them simultaneously. It also closes the refuel shutoff valve for a respective tank when it reaches half the total preselected value, completing refueling when the combined total equals the preselected value.

In Manual Refueling Mode, the REFUEL SELECTION Switch is set to MANUAL. The refueling personnel can open and close the Refuel Shutoff Valve via the TANK REFUELING Switch on the Refuel/defuel Control Panel. The manual shutoff function overrides the automatic shutoff function.

Bleed air is processed through two PACKs, where its temperature and pressure are adjusted. Hot trim air from upstream of the PACKs is mixed with air from the mixing manifold in the air conditioning distribution duct. The mixing manifold combines air from the PACKs and recirculation fans. Recirculation fans filter cabin air, sending part to the mixing manifold and the rest to the AFT cargo compartment for ventilation.
Integrated Air System Controll
When one PACK fails, the other PACK provides normal system operations, but limited to an altitude of 31000 ft.

If both PACKs fail, the flight altitude is limited to below 10000 ft and CAB ΔP is less than 1 psi. When these conditions are satisfied, sufficient fresh air can be provided to the cockpit and cabin through the emergency RAM air valve.

The system automatically enters Windshear Escape Mode (WS Mode) when the TAWS detects a windshear warning. Upon detection:
1.  **Entry:** The lateral Mode automatically switches to GA, and the vertical Mode switches to WS. The Autopilot (AP) disengages automatically after 2 seconds. The Flight Director (FD) will automatically engage.
2.  **Operation:** The system generates optimal escape maneuver commands based on airspeed, radio altitude, and AOA data. These commands continue until the windshear warnings cease. Thrust is set to TOGA.
3.  **Exit:**
    *   **Automatic:** The system exits WS Mode when windshear warnings cease.

The pilot must cancel the exit from course reversal holds used in instrument approach procedures before the FMS sequences to the inbound course INTC waypoint. After crossing the FIX, the FMS follows the complete holding pattern in the normal way. The FMS operates the aircraft to continue the hold by completing the turn to the outbound leg and continuing the hold, completing the turn to the inbound leg and continuing the hold, or continuing the hold as if the exit was never selected if the aircraft is on the inbound leg. Responses: Stall Protection System provides stall alert, stall protection and auto-ignition functions.
The Stall Protection System provides stall alert, stall protection, and auto-ignition functions.

The Stall Protection System (SPS) includes two Angle of Attack (AOA) Sensors integrated with Stall Protection Computers (SPC), and one stick pusher integrated in the AP pitch servo. It provides stall alert, stall protection, and auto-ignition functions. The SPS calculates AOA thresholds for these functions based on various inputs including AOA, flap angle, airspeed/Mach number, overload, ice signal, WING A/I Switch, STALL ADVANCE Switch, and WOW Signal. If ADC or IRU data is unavailable, it uses data from the Integrated Standby Instrument (ISI). When the current AOA reaches a threshold, the Stall Protection Computer (SPC) generates stall alert, stall shaker, and pusher commands, as well as auto-ignition control signals. Stick-pusher commands are sent to the autoflight system by the IPC, controlling the pitch servo to drive the elevator. Both SPCs must generate stall pusher commands simultaneously for the stick pusher to activate.
tall alert, stall protection and auto-ignitio

Each control column has one stick shaker and each Stall Protection Computer (SPC) can drive both stick shakers at the same time. When the current AOA of the aircraft reaches a threshold value for stall alert, the Stall Protection Computer (SPC) will generate a stall shaker command. The stick shaker activates when the airframe AOA is above its threshold and deactivates when the airframe AOA is less than the threshold decreased by 0.5°.
The Stall Protection Computer (SPC) commands the AP pitch servo to activate the stick pusher. Only when both SPCs generate stall pusher commands simultaneously will the stick pusher activate.
gle of Attack (AOA), FLAP angle, Airspeed/Mach number, Normal overload, side overload, Ice signal, WING A/I Switch signal, STALL ADVANCE Switch, WOW Signal.
Integrated Standby Instrument (ISI)
tall alert, stall shaker and pusher commands as well as auto-ignition control signal

The Stall Protection Computer (SPC) will generate a stall alert, stall shaker and pusher commands. The stick-push commands will be sent to the autoflight system by the IPC which controls the pitch servo to drive the elevator. Only when both SPC's generate stall pusher commands at the same time, will the stick pusher activate.
Stall Protection System provides stall alert, stall protection and auto-ignition functions.

The Stall Protection System (SPS) has several modes with decreasing priority: Flap/Slat System Fail Advance Mode, ADVANCE ON Mode, Ice Advance Mode 3, Ice Advance Mode 2, Ice Advance Mode 1, and normal Mode. In modes other than normal mode, the AOA threshold for stall alert, stall protection, and auto-ignition decreases, which enhances the stall protection margin. For example, the AOA of stall alert and stick pusher is the same between Ice Advance Mode 1 and Ice Advance Mode 2, and also between Ice Advance Mode 3 and ADVANCE ON Mode. However, the AOA threshold for Ice Advance Mode 1 and 2 is greater than that for Ice Advance Mode 3 and ADVANCE ON Mode. The ADVANCE ON Mode specifically drives stall alert functions (stick vibration, STALL aural alert, and warning flag on the PFD) and reduces stick pusher activation when the AOA returns to normal conditions.

The AOA of stall alert and stick pusher is the same between Ice Advance Mode 1 and Ice Advance Mode 2. It's also the same between Ice Advance Mode 3 and ADVANCE ON Mode. However the AOA of the former (Ice Advance Mode 1 and 2) is greater than that of the latter one (Ice Advance Mode 3 and ADVANCE ON Mode).
Ice Advance Mode 1 and Ice Advance Mode 2

Stall Protection System (SPS) Ice Advance Mode 1, activates in all of the following conditions: Ice detector on either side detects ice. – Wing anti-ice system available. STALL ADVANCE Switch is released.
Ice Advance Mode 2 activates when the ice detector on either side detects ice, the wing anti-ice system is available, and the STALL ADVANCE Switch is released.
Ice detector on either side detects ice. Wing Anti-Ice System fails. STALL ADVANCE Switch is released.
DVANCE ON Mode activates if the STALL ADVANCE Switch is pushed, and the ON light illuminates.

The Stall Protection System (SPS) enters Flap/Slat Fail Advance Mode in any of the following conditions:
- Flap system fails on FSECU bus, and flap configuration is not in 0.
- Flap system fails on FSECU bus or slat angle on both sides is not available, and flap configuration is not in 0.
- The slat angle difference between the two sides is 3° for 5 s, and flap configuration is not in 0.
When the conditions for Flap/Slat Fail Advance Mode are not satisfied, the Stall Protection System reverts to normal mode.

Stall Protection System (SPS) Ice Advance Mode 2 does not exit automatically. To exit, cycle the STALL ADVANCE Switch when the flap is down and the aircraft is in level flight. It also exits if a higher priority mode is triggered (Ice Advance Mode 3, Flap/Slat Fail Advance Mode, or ADVANCE ON Mode).
To exit Ice Advance Mode 2, when the flap is down and the aircraft is in level flight, the STALL ADVANCE Switch must be cycled. The SPS ICE MODE 2 message on the EICAS display will then disappear.

Ice Advance Mode 2 does not exit automatically. It remains active even if the conditions for its activation are no longer met, unless a higher priority mode is triggered or the STALL ADVANCE Switch is manipulated. To exit Ice Advance Mode 2 manually, the STALL ADVANCE Switch must be cycled when the aircraft is in level flight with flaps deployed.

If the STALL ADVANCE Switch on the overhead panel is pushed manually while in Ice Advance Mode 2, the Stall Protection System (SPS) enters ADVANCE ON Mode. If the STALL ADVANCE Switch is released manually, the SPS enters normal mode or Advance On Mode based on a logical judgment of the current status.

To exit Ice Advance Mode 2:
When flap is down and the aircraft is in level flight, cycle the STALL ADVANCE Switch. The SPS ICE MODE 2 message on the EICAS display disappears.
Ice Advance Mode 2 does not exit automatically. After the WING A/I Switch is engaged, the SPS enters Ice Advance Mode 2 and remains in this mode even if the WING A/I Switch is disconnected.
When the Stall Protection Computer (SPC) is powered on, Advance On Mode is not affected by aircraft air/ground status.
The stick pusher is activated when the Stall Protection Computer (SPC) sends a push command. For the stick pusher to engage, both SPCs must generate stall pusher commands simultaneously.

Bleed air from the pneumatic system is adjusted through two flow control valves, and temperature and pressure are adjusted through two PACKs. Then, the bleed air enters the mixing manifold where it is mixed with recirculated cabin air. Hot trim air from upstream of the PACK is mixed with the air from the mixing manifold in the air conditioning distribution duct, and then distributed to the cockpit and cabin.
cabin, cockpit, avionics compartment and cargo compartment

On the lower side of the cabin, the air is filtered by recirculation filters and extracted by two recirculation fans. Part of this recirculated air is sent to the mixing manifold to mix with fresh cold air from the PACK.
Part of the recirculated air is sent to the mixing manifold to mix with the fresh cold air from the PACK, and the rest is sent to the AFT cargo compartment for ventilation.
The flow of conditioned air is automatically controlled by the integrated air system controllers, which regulate the flow control valves.
bleed air shutoff and overheat protection, air conditioning system temperature regulation, and flow monitoring

The integrated air system controllers regulate the flow control valves by controlling the shutoff and overheat protection of bleed air, temperature regulation of the air conditioning system, and flow monitoring.

When one PACK fails, the other PACK provides normal system operations, but limited to an altitude of 31000 ft. Sufficient fresh air can be provided to the cockpit and cabin through the emergency RAM air valve.
The flow control valves can be closed by turning off the L(R) PACK Switch on the AIR CONDITION Control Panel.

Shorthand entries are resolved to only one degree of both latitude and longitude. They cannot be named and must have five characters. The letter N or E identifies positions in the Northern Hemisphere, with N indicating North latitude and West longitude, and E indicating North latitude and East longitude. The letters S and W identify positions in the Southern Hemisphere, with S indicating South latitude and East longitude, and W indicating South latitude and West longitude. The two-digit latitude always comes before longitude. The placement of the letter indicates the value of the longitude hundreds digit: in the third character position if longitude is 100° or greater, and at the end if longitude is less than 100°.

This differs from COM and NAV tuning where the outer knob adjusts integer digits and the inner knob adjusts decimal digits directly.

TCAS detects aircraft equipped with transponders in its vicinity, displays potential and predicted collision targets, and issues vertical maneuvering indications to avoid conflicts. It operates independently of ground-based ATC and has a detection range of up to 30-40 NM laterally and 9900 ft vertically. The display can show up to 30 aircraft simultaneously. TCAS interrogates transponders to determine an intruder's relative bearing, range, closure rate, and relative altitude, then computes its trajectory, Closest Point of Approach (CPA), and time to CPA. When a collision threat is present, aural and visual alerts are triggered, and TCAS optimizes vertical orders for separation. TCAS provides Traffic Advisories (TA) for proximate traffic that may become a threat, Preventive Resolution Advisories (PRA) to avoid deviation from the current path, and Corrective Resolution Advisories (CRA) to take action for threat aggravation. Intruder classification includes proximate traffic (no threat, within 6 NM and ±1200 ft), traffic advisory (potential threat, TAU ~40s), and resolution advisory (real threat, TAU ~25s). The TCAS display on the PFD/MFD shows intruder position, altitude (relative or absolute), and trend (climbing/descending). It also indicates TCAS mode/status (e.g., FAIL, OFF, TA ONLY, TA/RA).
